propositions.text: The Appellant, a Pakistani citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection, with no new evidence or oral hearing requested.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection, he has not submitted new evidence in support of his claim and he has not requested an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant requests the RPD decision be set aside and his claim allowed by the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant requests that the determination of the RPD be set aside and his claim be allowed by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

propositions.text: Alternatively, the Appellant requests the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration by a differently-constituted panel.
propositions.quote: Alternatively the Appellant requests that the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration by a differently-constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection without new evidence or oral hearing; the Appellant requests the decision be set aside or remitted.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Division (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges he is a Shia Muslim active in his religious community.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged he is a Shia Muslim who served as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and was active in his religious community.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he is a Shia Muslim active in his religious community.

propositions.text: The Appellant left Pakistan in 2009 fearing for his life due to conflict with his brothers over his father's estate.
propositions.quote: He left Pakistan in 2009 because he feared his life was at risk from his brothers as a result of conflict over his father's estate.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant left Pakistan in 2009 fearing for his life from his brothers over estate conflict.

propositions.text: He travelled to the UK on a study visa in 2009 and attended school until 2011 when it closed; visa expired in 2012.
propositions.quote: He travelled to the United Kingdom (UK) on a study visa on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and attended a school until 2011 when the school closed. His study visa expired on XXXX XXXX, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant travelled to the UK on a study visa in 2009, attended school until 2011, and his visa expired in 2012.

propositions.text: He returned to Pakistan in 2011 for about a month and a half and resolved problems with his brothers.
propositions.quote: He returned to Pakistan for a visit in XXXX 2011 for approximately a month and a half, and his problems with his brothers were resolved.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant returned to Pakistan in 2011 for a short visit and resolved issues with his brothers.

propositions.text: He made an unsuccessful refugee claim in the UK in 2012 and was deported to Pakistan in 2014.
propositions.quote: He made an unsuccessful refugee claim in the UK in XXXX 2012, and he was deported to Pakistan in XXXX 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant made an unsuccessful UK refugee claim in 2012 and was deported to Pakistan in 2014.

propositions.text: In Pakistan, he resumed supporting the local Imam and started receiving threatening calls in 2014.
propositions.quote: In Pakistan he resumed his activities in support of the local Imam XXXX and started receiving threatening calls from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2014.

paragraphs.summary: In Pakistan, the Appellant resumed supporting the local Imam and began receiving threats in 2014.

propositions.text: He was assaulted in 2014 and threatened with death if he continued community activities; threats extended to family after coming to Canada.
propositions.quote: He was assaulted on XXXX XXXX, 2014 and told he would be killed if he continued to ignore the XXXX demand to stop his community activities. Threats were made to his family as well even after he came to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant was assaulted and threatened in 2014, with threats continuing to his family after arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: He fears the XXXX and states police protection and internal flight alternative are unavailable.
propositions.quote: He fears the XXXX and states that protection from the police is not available and there is no internal flight alternative available to him.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant fears the XXXX and says police protection and internal flight alternative are unavailable.

propositions.text: The RPD panel identified credibility as the determinative issue in the claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD panel indicates that the determinative issue in this claim is credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD panel found credibility to be the determinative issue in the claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the issues are the appropriate standard of review and whether the RPD erred in credibility findings including documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the issues in this appeal are: * What is the appropriate standard of review? * Did the RPD err in its credibility findings, including the credibility of documentary evidence adduced in support of the claim?

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the issues are the standard of review and alleged RPD errors in credibility findings.

propositions.text: IRPA sets out grounds and remedies for appeal but does not specify the RAD's standard of review.
propositions.quote: While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA provides appeal grounds but not the RAD's standard of review.

propositions.text: The RAD now benefits from Federal Court jurisprudence on its role relative to the RPD.
propositions.quote: The RAD now has the benefit of Federal Court jurisprudence which speaks to the appellate tribunal's role in relation to that of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RAD benefits from Federal Court jurisprudence on its role relative to the RPD.

propositions.text: Huruglica holds the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal, reviewing all aspects and deferring to RPD only where it has particular advantage.
propositions.quote: In Huruglica, the Court determined that the RAD is to conduct a "hybrid appeal." It is to review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, deferring to the RPD only where the lower tribunal enjoys a particular advantage in reaching a conclusion.

propositions.text: Where the RAD's assessment differs from the RPD's, the RAD must substitute its own determination.
propositions.quote: Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

paragraphs.summary: Huruglica holds the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal, deferring to RPD only where it has advantage; RAD substitutes its own decision if differing.

propositions.text: The RAD can respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not restricted to intervening only for palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: The Court determined that, in conducting its assessment, the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. The RAD is, however, not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on the facts only where there is "palpable and overriding error."

paragraphs.summary: The RAD may respect RPD credibility findings but is not limited to intervening only for palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: The RAD will review all RPD evidence and independently assess refugee or protection status.
propositions.quote: The RAD will review all of the evidence in the RPD record and come to its own independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will independently review all evidence and assess refugee or protection status.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the Appellant's brief analysis of the standard of review aligns with the RAD's view.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant submits a brief analysis of his view of the appropriate standard of review which reflects the RAD's view as stated above.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant's standard of review analysis aligns with the RAD's view.

propositions.text: The RPD panel noted the Appellant claimed risk in Pakistan due to religious activities and questioned his religious activities in the UK from 2009 to 2014.
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant stated he was at risk in Pakistan because of his religious activities. The panel questioned the Appellant as to his religious activities in the UK from 2009 to 2014.

propositions.text: The Appellant said he attended mosque for Friday prayers whenever he had time, about four times a month.
propositions.quote: The Appellant responded he went to the mosque for Friday prayers whenever he had time. He further stated he went four times a month.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD panel noted the Appellant's claimed risk from religious activities and questioned his UK religious attendance; he said he attended mosque about four times monthly.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant testified he intended to serve his religious community in the UK but was unable to spare time and thought his problems resulted from lack of service.
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant testified that he pinned to serve his religious community during his four and a half years in the UK, but he was unable to spare the time. He was deported in 2014 and thought his problems in the UK resulted from his lack of service to his religion and the community.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified he went to the majlis only once every two months.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further testified he went to the majlis only once in two months.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant testified he intended to serve his religious community but lacked time; he attended majlis once every two months.

propositions.text: The panel asked the Appellant for corroborating evidence of UK religious observance such as a letter, photograph or receipt.
propositions.quote: The panel asked the Appellant if he had any corroborating evidence of his UK religious observance such as a letter from the Imam XXXX, a photograph or a receipt.

propositions.text: The Appellant responded he did not do anything in the UK and donations were made by his wife in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: The Appellant responded he did not do anything there and donations were made by his wife in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The panel asked the Appellant for UK religious observance evidence; the Appellant said he did nothing there and his wife made donations in Pakistan.

propositions.text: The panel drew a negative credibility inference from the Appellant's lack of UK religious involvement inconsistent with alleged Pakistan activities.
propositions.quote: The panel drew a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility with regards to the lack of involvement in religious activities in the UK seemed inconsistent with his alleged activities in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant's lack of UK religious involvement inconsistent with his Pakistan activities, harming his credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits lack of UK religious involvement does not discredit his Pakistan religious activism.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits his lack of involvement in religious activity in the UK does not inherently indicate his stated religious activism in Pakistan lacks credibility.

propositions.text: The Appellant explains difficulty balancing community service with work and study in the UK.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits he explained he had difficulty sparing enough time for community service while working and studying in the UK.

propositions.text: The Appellant notes his testimony was consistent with his Basis of Claim narrative.
propositions.quote: The Appellant notes his testimony was consistent with his BOC narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues his UK inactivity does not discredit Pakistan activism, citing work-study constraints and consistent testimony.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding of evolving UK religious activity testimony was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the panel's finding that his testimony concerning his account of his religious activities in the UK seemed to evolve was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's finding that his UK religious testimony evolved was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's demand for objective corroboration of low-level UK religious activity was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also submits the panel's requirement of objective corroboration concerning his religious activities in the UK, given his admittedly low level of involvement, was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's requirement for objective corroboration of minimal UK religious activity was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference about UK Shia community lack is unreasonable given circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference concerning his lack of involvement in the UK Shia community is unreasonable in light of the circumstances noted above.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant contends the panel's negative credibility inference about his UK Shia community lack is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD reviewed evidence and notes the panel made no specific findings on lack of corroboration or evolving testimony.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the panel made no specific findings concerning the lack of corroborating documentation and the Appellant's evolving testimony in this regard.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Appellant's lack of substantive UK religious activity for 4.5 years raises doubt about his commitment to Shia Islam and concurs with the panel.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, in the context of the Appellant's evidence concerning his commitment to Shia Islam and his alleged religious activities in Pakistan, that the Appellant's lack of any substantive religious activity for approximately four and a half years in the UK raises a doubt concerning his evidence about his commitment to Shia Islam and the Shia community. The RAD concurs with the panel's finding in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant's 4.5-year UK religious inactivity raises doubt about his Shia commitment and concurs with the panel.

propositions.text: The panel noted a UK Home Office document suggesting false documents were submitted to extend study visa.
propositions.quote: The panel noted a UK Home Office document2 that suggested he submitted false documents indicating he was still attending school when this was not the case, and seeking an extension of his study visa.

propositions.text: The Appellant explained he contacted a lawyer for visa extension and false documents were attached without his knowledge.
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained he contacted a lawyer regarding an extension of his visa, and false documentation was attached to the application. The Appellant further explained that he was not informed about the use of false documentation.

propositions.text: The Appellant stated he knew it was a criminal act but took no responsibility and was surprised by UK immigration officials.
propositions.quote: He stated as well he was aware this was a criminal act but he took no responsibility and he was surprised when he was informed about this by UK immigration officials.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted false documents for visa extension; the Appellant said a lawyer attached them without his knowledge and he took no responsibility.

propositions.text: The panel found the Appellant was the only beneficiary of false documents and did not believe he was unaware of their use.
propositions.quote: The panel indicated that the Appellant was the only party benefiting from the false documentation and found that it did not believe the Appellant was unaware of the use of documentation indicating he was still enrolled in school when he was not.

propositions.text: The panel drew a negative inference about the Appellant's credibility regarding false documentation.
propositions.quote: The panel drew a negative inference in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant benefited from false documents and was likely aware, drawing a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding about false documents is unreasonable due to lawyer dependence and irrelevance to core claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the panel's finding in this regard is unreasonable. The Appellant notes his dependence on a Pakistani lawyer and the misrepresentations do not go to the heart of his claim in Canada which concerns incidents of religious persecution in Pakistan and not in the UK.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the misrepresentations were not necessarily determinative of credibility of material incidents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits the misrepresentations were not necessarily determinative of the credibility of such material incidents.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's finding on false documents is unreasonable and irrelevant to his core persecution claim in Canada.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees UK incidents do not go to core refugee claim but finds misrepresentations raise doubt about general credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees the incidents in the UK do not go to the core of the Appellant's refugee claim in Canada. The RAD finds however that the Appellant's misrepresentations in the UK do raise a doubt about his general credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Appellant's claim of unawareness of fraudulent documents strains credulity given visa application context.
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds in this regard that the Appellant's testimony that he was unaware of the fraudulent nature of documentation attached to the extension application strains credulity as he was making an application for the extension of his student visa when he knew he was no longer studying in a college.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds UK misrepresentations raise general credibility doubts and the Appellant's unawareness claim strains credulity.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant filed a UK form indicating he was single and childless, which was false.
propositions.quote: The panel noted that in a form he filed with the UK government3 he indicated he was single and without children when this was not the case.

propositions.text: The Appellant explained a consultant advised him to lie about marital status to avoid visa denial due to past refusals and fear.
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained a consultant advised him he would be denied a visa if he indicated he was married. He noted he had been denied a visa twice in the past and he feared another rejection.

propositions.text: The Appellant stated the consultant misguided him and he had no other option as he was in danger.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further stated the consultant misguided him but he noted he had no other option as he was in danger.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant falsely declared single on UK form; the Appellant said a consultant advised this due to visa fears and danger.

propositions.text: The panel found the Appellant willing to say whatever suited him to immigration authorities.
propositions.quote: The panel indicated the Appellant's testimony indicates he was willing to say whatever suited his convenience when dealing with immigration authorities.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant's UK lawyer said he was tortured and could be a victim again; the Appellant was unsure what this meant.
propositions.quote: The panel noted in the hearing that the Appellant's lawyer in the UK indicated the Appellant has been the subject of torture and can be a victim again. The Appellant was asked what this referred to and he responded "I am not sure."

propositions.text: The Appellant later testified he was beaten by his brothers in Pakistan in 2011.
propositions.quote: Subsequently he testified he had been beaten by his brothers during a visit to Pakistan in 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant willing to say anything to immigration; noted lawyer's torture claim and Appellant's 2011 beating testimony.

propositions.text: The panel noted no mention of torture in the Basis of Claim and drew a negative inference from inconsistent information.
propositions.quote: The panel noted there was no mention of torture in the Appellant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC) and drew a negative inference form the Appellant's inability to provide consistent and coherent information in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The panel drew a negative inference from the Appellant's failure to mention torture in his Basis of Claim and inconsistent information.

propositions.text: The panel asked why the 2011 beating was not mentioned; the Appellant said he told counsel's interpreter and forgot due to stress.
propositions.quote: The panel asked the Appellant why he did not mention he was beaten by his brothers in 2011. The Appellant responded he told his counsel's interpreter that he was beaten many times, he was detained a few times in the UK and he was under a lot of stress at the time.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified his beating and mistreatment slipped his mind when writing the Basis of Claim narrative.
propositions.quote: He further testified his beating in Pakistan and mistreatment in England slipped his mind when writing his BOC narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant said he told his interpreter about beatings and forgot to include them in his Basis of Claim due to stress.

propositions.text: The panel drew a negative inference from omissions due to lack of medical documentation explaining forgetfulness.
propositions.quote: The panel indicated, in the absence of any medical documentation explaining the Appellant's forgetfulness, it drew a negative inference from these omissions.

paragraphs.summary: The panel drew a negative inference from the Appellant's omissions without medical explanation for forgetfulness.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the Appellant makes no submission regarding the negative inference from omissions.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes the Appellant makes no submission in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant made no submission about the negative inference from omissions.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant's study visa expired in 2012, possibly in 2011 when school closed.
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant's study visa expired on XXXX XXXX, 2012, although it was arguable his student status expired in 2011 when the school closed.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant remained in the UK working illegally until arrested and then claimed refugee status in 2012.
propositions.quote: The panel further noted the Appellant remained in the UK working illegally until he was arrested and then made a refugee claim in XXXX 2012, alleging he was at risk from his brothers.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant overstayed his visa, worked illegally, was arrested, then claimed refugee status in 2012.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant claimed protection only after arrest and his illegal stay negatively impacts credibility and shows lack of subjective fear.
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant made his claim for protection only after his arrest. The panel further noted the Appellant's willingness to remain illegally in the UK and at risk of deportation negatively impacts on his credibility and shows a lack of subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant's delayed claim and illegal stay negatively affect credibility and show lack of subjective fear.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding on overstay does not reasonably lead to adverse credibility regarding Pakistan persecution incidents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the panel's finding in this regard does not reasonably lead to its adverse finding regarding the credibility of his evidence concerning incidents of persecution in Pakistan.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits overstay does not reasonably lead to lack of subjective fear about persecution incidents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits his overstay in the UK did not reasonably lead to a lack of subjective fear regarding the incidents of persecution.

propositions.text: The Appellant notes the panel failed to distinguish between incidents prompting UK stay and those prompting Canada claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant notes the panel failed to distinguish between the incidents and circumstances that prompted the Appellant to go to the UK and those that prompted him to come to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's overstay finding does not justify adverse credibility or lack of fear about Pakistan persecution and failed to distinguish incidents.

propositions.text: Appellant's UK overstay does not reasonably affect credibility about persecution incidents in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the Appellant that his overstay in the UK does not reasonably lead to an adverse finding regarding the credibility of his evidence concerning incidents of persecution in Pakistan

propositions.text: Appellant's UK overstay raises doubt about his general credibility
propositions.quote: The RAD finds however that the Appellant's actions in this regard in the UK does raise a further doubt about his general credibility

propositions.text: Letters from the Imam XXXX are relevant to credibility assessment
propositions.quote: The letters from the Imam XXXX

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the appellant's UK overstay does not affect credibility about persecution but raises general credibility doubts; letters from Imam XXXX are relevant.

propositions.text: Appellant corroborated fear with a 2015 letter from president of Imam XXXX
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant corroborated his fear of the XXXX with a XXXX XXXX, 2015 letter allegedly written by a person who described himself as the president of the Imam XXXX

propositions.text: Letter indicated threats due to conversion to Shia faith
propositions.quote: The letter indicated the Appellant faced threats from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX due to his conversion to the Shia faith

propositions.text: Appellant claimed to be Shia from birth, not convert
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant claimed to be a Shia from birth, and that it was the XXXX and not XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who is the agent of persecution

propositions.text: Appellant had brother seek replacement letter after inconsistencies
propositions.quote: When the Appellant was made aware of the inconsistencies he had his brother seek a replacement letter which was mailed on XXXX XXXX, 2015

propositions.text: Letter writer said he wrote letter for someone else but sent it to appellant by mistake
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained the letter writer indicated that he had written the letter for someone else but sent it to the Appellant by mistake

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted appellant's fear corroborated by a 2015 letter with inconsistencies; appellant claimed Shia from birth and sought replacement letter after errors.

propositions.text: Second letter explained errors as 'a typo mistake on my part'
propositions.quote: The panel noted the second letter indicated that the letter writer explained the errors were due to "a typo mistake on my part."

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the second letter explained errors as a typographical mistake by the letter writer.

propositions.text: Initial letter accurate in many respects including naming appellant and noting threats
propositions.quote: The panel noted in the hearing that the initial letter was accurate in many respects as it named the Appellant, indicated he served as general secretary of the Imam XXXX in 2009 and noted the beatings and threats

propositions.text: Appellant explained initial letter noted conversion because it was written for someone else
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained the letter was written for someone else

propositions.text: Appellant did not know why mistake made about agent of persecution; letter writer said he made a mistake
propositions.quote: The Appellant responded he did not know and noted the letter writer had indicated he made a mistake

propositions.text: Appellant said letter writer said he cut and pasted from another case
propositions.quote: Subsequently the Appellant stated he called the letter writer and he said this happened to someone else and he cut and pasted

paragraphs.summary: Panel found initial letter accurate but appellant said it was written for someone else; appellant gave evolving explanations for errors.

propositions.text: Appellant said discrepancies due to letter written for someone else
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant explained the discrepancies in the first letter were the result of the letter having been written for someone else

propositions.text: Letter writer said discrepancies were 'a typo mistake on my part'
propositions.quote: this was not what the letter writer said in the second letter in which it was indicated the discrepancies were "a typo mistake on my part."

paragraphs.summary: Panel noted appellant's explanation of discrepancies differs from letter writer's explanation of typographical error.

propositions.text: Appellant's explanations evolved and typographical error explanation not persuasive
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant's explanations for the discrepancy seemed to evolve, no explanation was provided as to why much of the initial letter apparently was accurate and the explanation of a typographical error is not persuasive regarding the issues of conversion and the agent of persecution

paragraphs.summary: Panel found appellant's evolving explanations unpersuasive and typographical error explanation insufficient.

propositions.text: Two letters are completely unreliable and possibly fraudulent
propositions.quote: The panel found the two letters are completely unreliable, and possibly fraudulent, and it accorded them no weight

propositions.text: Panel drew negative inference on appellant's credibility from letters
propositions.quote: In addition the panel drew a negative inference in this regard as to the Appellant's credibility

paragraphs.summary: Panel found letters unreliable and possibly fraudulent, drawing negative credibility inference against appellant.

propositions.text: Panel's negative credibility inference is unreasonable
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference in this regard is unreasonable

propositions.text: Letter writer provided reasonable explanation for errors
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits the letter writer provided a reasonable explanation for the errors in the original letter

propositions.text: Panel's phrase is ambiguous or unintelligible, casting doubt on findings
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits the panel's use of the phrase "...the panel again and I hate and lovely day is that okay into..." are somewhat ambiguous and/or unintelligible and as such casts doubt on the reliability of its findings

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues panel's negative credibility inference is unreasonable, letter writer's explanation reasonable, and panel's phrase ambiguous.

propositions.text: RAD not persuaded letter writer's explanation was reasonable
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded that the letter writer provided a reasonable explanation for the errors in the original letter

propositions.text: Panel did not err in findings about letters and discrepancies
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the panel did not err in its findings concerning the letters and the explanations for the discrepancy

propositions.text: RAD agrees with panel's analysis regarding letters and discrepancies
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the panel's analysis in this regard

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds letter writer's explanation unreasonable and agrees with panel's findings and analysis on letters and discrepancies.

propositions.text: RAD agrees panel's phrase is ambiguous and reflects poor proofreading
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the Appellant as to the ambiguity and/or unintelligible nature of the panel's phrase cited above

propositions.text: Phrase does not cast doubt on reliability of panel's findings
propositions.quote: The RAD finds however that this phrase reflects poor proof reading by the panel and it does not cast doubt on the reliability of its findings in this regard

paragraphs.summary: RAD agrees panel's phrase is ambiguous due to poor proofreading but it does not affect reliability of findings.

propositions.text: Appellant provided medical report dated XXXX XXXX, 2014 about injuries from beating
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Appellant provided a medical report dated XXXX XXXX, 2014, allegedly pertaining to injuries received in a beating

paragraphs.summary: Panel noted appellant provided a 2014 medical report about injuries from a beating.

propositions.text: Appellant testified mother got fraudulent medical document to restore peace
propositions.quote: The panel further noted the Appellant testified that his mother was able to get a doctor to misrepresent that she had a XXXX XXXX to assist her restoring peace among her sons

propositions.text: Appellant acknowledged mother's medical document was fraudulent
propositions.quote: The Appellant acknowledged his mother's medical document was fraudulent

propositions.text: Panel noted ease of obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The panel noted as well the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan

propositions.text: Appellant did not explain why his medical document should be considered authentic
propositions.quote: The panel also noted the Appellant did not explain why his medical document should be considered authentic when his mother's document was not

paragraphs.summary: Panel noted appellant's testimony about mother's fraudulent document and ease of fraud in Pakistan; appellant did not explain authenticity of his own document.

propositions.text: Ease of obtaining fraudulent documents does not render appellant's medical report inauthentic
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan does not necessarily render his medical report inauthentic

propositions.text: Mother's fraudulent document does not indicate appellant's document is fraudulent
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits the fraudulent nature of his mother's medical document does not necessarily indicate his own medical document is fraudulent

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues ease of fraud and mother's fraudulent document do not prove his medical report is fraudulent.

propositions.text: Panel failed to make definitive finding on authenticity of appellant's medical report
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits as well the panel failed to make a definitive finding as to the authenticity of the report pertaining to the Appellant as it was required to do and this is a reviewable error

paragraphs.summary: Appellant submits panel erred by not definitively finding on authenticity of his medical report.

propositions.text: RAD agrees ease of fraud and mother's fraudulent document do not mean appellant's medical report is fraudulent
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the Appellant that the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan and the fraudulent nature of the Appellant's mother's medical document does not necessarily mean the Appellant's medical document is fraudulent

propositions.text: RAD agrees panel did not make definitive finding on authenticity of appellant's medical document
propositions.quote: The RAD further agrees with the Appellant that the panel does not make a definitive finding regarding the authenticity or fraudulent nature of his medical document

paragraphs.summary: RAD agrees with appellant that ease of fraud does not prove his medical report fraudulent and panel made no definitive finding on it.

propositions.text: Medical document shows history of assault but no evidence on perpetrators or reasons
propositions.quote: The RAD notes this document indicates under the title "Description of Injuries" the words "History of Assault" followed by a list of injuries. The RAD further notes there is no evidence in this document as to the perpetrators of the assault or the reasons for it

propositions.text: RAD gives medical document little evidentiary weight on central issue
propositions.quote: The RAD gives this document little evidentiary weight as to the central issue in this appeal

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds medical document shows assault history but lacks perpetrator or reason evidence and gives it little weight.

propositions.text: Panel found appellant not credible witness
propositions.quote: The panel found, on the basis of credibility findings noted above, that the Appellant was not a credible witness

propositions.text: Panel found appellant's allegations of attack and risk in Pakistan not true
propositions.quote: The panel further found the Appellant's allegations that he was attacked and threatened and faces risks in Pakistan are not true

propositions.text: Panel concluded appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence for positive claim determination
propositions.quote: The panel concluded that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to allow a positive determination of his claim

paragraphs.summary: Panel found appellant not credible, allegations untrue, and insufficient credible evidence for positive claim.

propositions.text: Panel did not provide good reasons for rebutting presumption of truthfulness
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the panel did not provide good or valid reasons for effectively finding that the presumption of truthfulness to which he is entitled has been rebutted

paragraphs.summary: Appellant submits panel failed to provide valid reasons for rebutting presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: RAD finds appellant's untruthfulness and delay in UK claim raise doubt about general credibility
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the Appellant's record of untruthfulness and his delay in making a claim for protection in the UK until he was arrested raises a doubt as to his general credibility

propositions.text: Disclosure of likely fraudulent letters and explanation discrepancies rebut presumption of truthfulness
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds that the Appellant's disclosure of two letters that are likely fraudulent and the discrepancy in his explanation from that provided by the letter writer is sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness regarding his allegations

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds appellant's untruthfulness, delay, and likely fraudulent letters rebut presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: RAD agrees appellant failed to provide sufficient credible evidence for positive claim decision
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the panel that the Appellant has failed to provide sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to allow a positive decision in regard to his claim

paragraphs.summary: RAD agrees appellant failed to provide sufficient credible evidence for positive claim decision.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA , the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and dismisses the appeal, as stated by the court.
